name: Emeka Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Emeka, 58, a lead developer at a tech company that tracks streetlight faults. I have a master's degree and know the pole maps well; I use AI now and then after a colleague has shown me a check that matches crew orders. A false closure across the road once left the school crossing dark. My partner works part-time as a school caretaker, our children are grown, and we have a modest mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the streetlight crew that a dark-lamp report needs the pole number and a real repair visit. I lead software for a tech company's lighting-fault system and use AI now and then to draft test cases after a colleague has shown a reliable method.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI changes little, I expect my lead role and income to continue. I have a master's degree and typical senior pay, my partner works part-time as a school caretaker, we have four months of expenses saved, and some similar firms are nearby; we still pay a modest mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking closed lamp faults against crew work orders and the pole map. Starting next month, we'd save 85 extra each month while both wages hold and the mortgage stays current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job in this version. A green dot on a map does not light a crossing for a child walking home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the work order show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dashboard closed a lamp fault after a crew visited the wrong pole across the road. The work order had a different number, so I reopened the correct fault before the evening school run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your children fund the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children live on their own. They tell us which crossings are dark, but their pay is not our mortgage fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may write fault code and answer residents, but a lamp should not be closed because a crew fixed the pole across the road. I would test the new checks against the crew's paper order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My team could become smaller even though I lead it. Four months saved buys some time, but my partner's part-time caretaker wage would not cover the mortgage and all household costs alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager for paid time to learn the AI pole-matching check that our senior tester has already used on old cases. If the manager agrees and it catches the wrong-pole visit without reopening a genuinely fixed lamp, I'd use it on one district release with a crew supervisor able to stop closure; we'd defer a planned garden shed until paid staffing hours are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours, but I will learn a check if somebody can show me both sorts of outcome. A tidy map should not overrule the crew standing at the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which two lamp cases matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wrong-pole case has two numbers one digit apart. The correctly fixed lamp must stay closed; otherwise crews will be sent back for work they have already done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why can the shed wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shed can wait because our tools still fit in the garage. We would keep the cash until the firm writes down how many paid hours my team gets.

I'd keep **supervisor stop power** on live fault closures.

I cannot cover **mortgage and bills** on part-time caretaker wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write lighting code before street-repair robots arrive around 2031. A resident still needs to report the lamp that stays dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead post could be cut quickly when cheaper software makes and tests routine closures. My partner's caretaker wage will not cover the mortgage and food alone, and four months saved is a search window, not a retirement fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the local utility and three nearby firms about actual paid fault-review or software vacancies, wages and hours. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed post whose wage with my partner's actual shifts covers mortgage, food and travel; if none qualifies, I'd seek other available paid local work while using savings and call the lender before an instalment is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing the larger wage before another post is signed. A street full of lamps does not mean the utility has a job for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you show another employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show an anonymised wrong-pole correction with the two pole numbers and work order. It explains why the crew's visit could not close the reported fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How could shifts change household pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner needs the new shift hours in writing. If a move or schedule change ends the paid school-caretaker shifts, my wage alone has to cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 might let me find a paid utility job at the regional headquarters, but thinking AI could still reach my code before street robots around 2034. Moving does not make the technology disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The headquarters has more fault records than our small town, yet I cannot assume a vacancy. My partner would have to leave school-caretaker shifts, and four months saved cannot cover a new deposit and moving van without help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the regional utility for posted paid fault-review duties, salary, start date and relocation terms, then discuss the actual offer with my partner. If there is a signed vacancy, the employer pays deposit and moving costs, my wage alone covers new housing, food and travel until my partner finds work, and my partner agrees, we'd move after 2031; otherwise I'd keep paid development while available and seek local paid work if cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the post and the cost of a move, but five years lets us compare real numbers. I won't count my partner's school-caretaker wage after we leave town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which utility duty would matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The utility's job description should say whether I can reopen a false closure after the crew reports a different pole. I would not trade our home for a role that only repeats a dashboard status.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would your partner resign?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would need the signed start date and deposit payment before resigning from the school. Our grown children might visit, but we are not assuming a spare room or their wages at the new place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 might bring me to 68, but thinking AI still reaches lighting code before street robots around 2039. A streetlight crew's work order should remain readable after I stop writing the fault software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Today two wages and four months saved keep the mortgage manageable. I have not verified either retirement amount, and I cannot assume a regional utility move or my partner's future shifts will happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wrong-pole test and save 85 monthly while both wages hold, then request both retirement statements and compare verified income with mortgage, food and travel. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if those figures cover bills; otherwise I'd keep or seek available paid work without counting our grown children's wages or an unoffered move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about distant work, but the present mortgage gets paid. A ten-year warning is useful only when we check real wages and statements along the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you leave in the record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The record would keep both pole numbers, the wrong crew visit and the later correct repair. A new developer should see why the dashboard was green too early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help with a move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children have homes elsewhere. We like their visits, but they do not owe us a relocation deposit or retirement pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the firm could cut lead code work before a utility or nearby company offers paid fault review. Written notice, real paid vacancies and an early lender conversation would help protect the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a green map means a light is on. A child crossing after school sees the actual lamp, not our dashboard; the crew's work order has to match the pole.

headlineQuote: A child crossing after school sees the actual lamp, not our dashboard; the crew's work order has to match the pole.

biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his larger wage before another paid fault-review post appears.
